content: 1. The age Z-score was assessed over a 7-month follow-up period. Measurements of recumbent length were taken to the nearest millimeter by trained staff using a measuring board. The initial measurement was conducted in September 2002, and a follow-up measurement was performed 7 months later during survey administration. Age was determined using the IPTc trial database specific to the study area. 2. Linear growth was evaluated over a 7-month follow-up period. Recumbent length was measured to the nearest millimeter by trained staff using a measuring board in September 2002. The average duration of the interval under study was 7 months. In some cases, standing height was used instead of recumbent length. 3. Anemia was assessed using blood samples obtained via heel or ring finger puncture. Capillary blood was collected in a microcuvette, and hemoglobin concentration was measured directly using a portable hemoglobinometer (HemoCue®). A hemoglobin concentration of less than 11 g/dL was used as the diagnostic threshold for anemia. 4. Fruit consumption was not significantly associated with anemia prevalence when considering consumption within the past 24 hours. However, when comparing daily versus less-than-daily fruit consumption frequencies, a significant association with anemia prevalence was observed. Individuals consuming fruit less than daily had greater odds of anemia compared to those consuming fruit daily. 5. Complementary feeding practices and nutritional status of children aged 6–23 months were studied in Aceh, Indonesia. This cross-sectional study included 392 healthy children and was conducted between May and June 2016. Mothers provided information on the frequency of fruit, animal-source food (ASF), and non-plant-source (NPS) consumption through three repeated 24-hour recalls. Frequency of fruit consumption was categorized as ≥3 times/week, 1–2 times/week, or never. 6. A study conducted in rural Senegal included 543 children aged 6–42 months who were part of the Intermittent Preventive Malaria Treatment in children (IPTc) trial. Measurements of height and weight were taken in September 2002 and again 7 months later during survey administration. Caregivers provided details on the frequency of fruit and ASF consumption using 24-hour recalls. Frequency was defined as 0–2 days/week or ≥3 days/week. Another definition categorized consumption as rare or frequent, though this was not further clarified in the study. 7. A cross-sectional study in Brazil included 205 children aged 6–12 months living in Viçosa, Minas Gerais. The study was conducted between July 2002 and April 2003. Frequency of fruit, ASF, and NPS consumption was measured using a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) and 24-hour recall. Anemia was defined as hemoglobin <11 g/dL. The study had a poor-to-fair rating due to limited methodological details, lack of sample size justification, and absence of baseline characteristics for the study sample. 8. A longitudinal cohort study in Norway followed 9,025 mother-infant pairs from 18 months to 7 years of age. Frequency of fruit and vegetable consumption was measured using a questionnaire at three time points (18 months, 36 months, and 7 years). Frequency was categorized into low, medium, and high, with high defined as >14 times/week. 9. The frequency of legume and bean consumption was not significantly associated with wasting, being underweight, or stunting. Age was determined through interviews with the infant’s mother. The certainty of evidence for these outcomes was downgraded due to serious concerns about imprecision and indirectness. 10. The consumption of beans was not significantly associated with anemia prevalence. Daily versus less-than-daily consumption frequencies were compared, and no significant differences were observed. 11. Overall, many of the studies reviewed had limitations, including small sample sizes, lack of adjustment for confounding variables, and insufficient methodological details. These factors contributed to downgrading the certainty of evidence for various outcomes.
